analysis.one_liner: Exempts stores and distributors from lawsuits over defective products they merely resold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Under long-standing product liability rules, a person hurt by a defective product can hold anyone in the chain of sale responsible — including the store that sold it — without proving that seller did anything wrong. This bill would have changed that. A store or distributor that only sold the product could not be sued at all, unless the injured person could prove the seller also manufactured it, helped design or install it, or altered it or gave a warranty the maker didn't authorize. Even then, the seller could only be sued for negligence, and only for the harm that specific act directly caused. The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees [S5], never received a hearing or vote, and expired at the end of the 109th Congress [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Retailers, distributors, and other product sellers. They would be shielded from strict liability — the no-fault rule that lets an injured person hold a seller responsible for a dangerous product without proving fault. The bill's own findings say sellers face higher insurance and litigation costs from being drawn into lawsuits over products they didn't make [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Exempts any lawful seller of a product from liability for injuries, monetary loss, or property damage arising from that product, unless the claimant proves the seller manufactured it, participated in its design or installation, or altered, modified, or expressly warranted it in a way the manufacturer did not authorize [S2][S3].
Even when a seller performed one of those extra activities, the claimant must prove the activity was negligent, and damages are limited to the harm directly caused by that activity [S2][S3].

The bill's stated rationale is that sellers are dragged into litigation over products they did not cause and bear higher insurance costs as a result, and that limiting their liability would lessen burdens on interstate commerce [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products. If the maker is foreign, insolvent, or hard to sue, the seller was often the remaining defendant with the money to pay a judgment; the bill would foreclose that route and force injured people to prove negligence against a seller to recover anything.

drawbacks.text: Injured consumers would lose strict liability against sellers — the rule that makes recovery possible without proving fault — and would instead have to prove a seller was negligent in a specific non-sale activity, with damages capped at what that activity directly caused [S2][S3].

Because sellers can be sued today even for products made by others, they currently have a financial reason to stock safe products and drop dangerous ones; the bill would remove that incentive [S3] — and where a manufacturer is insolvent, foreign, or beyond a court's reach, the seller was often the only practical defendant.
The bill would override state product liability law nationwide, replacing each state's rules for sellers with a single federal shield, applied to all products sold after enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a fair argument on the seller's side: a store that merely resells a product did not cause the defect, and many states already apply some form of an 'innocent seller' rule. But the federal version goes further — it removes strict liability from the entire retail chain and leaves injured people chasing manufacturers who may be absent, foreign, or insolvent, while weakening the market pressure retailers face to sell safe goods. The bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh these tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, sent to a subcommittee in June 2006, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Ric Keller introduced the bill on May 25, 2006, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
On June 5, 2006, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection; no further action of any kind was recorded [S5].
The bill gathered 23 cosponsors, 21 Republicans and 2 Democrats, but never received a markup, floor vote, or companion Senate action before the 109th Congress expired on January 3, 2007 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, people injured by defective products kept their existing right to hold sellers responsible under state liability law, and retailers did not get the federal shield they sought.

for.name: Rep. Ric Keller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 23 cosponsors, including original cosponsors from both parties.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chaired by Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner (R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no markup, no vote to send the bill to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection (House Energy and Commerce)
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred on June 5, 2006
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it was the last recorded stop in the bill's history.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 23 cosponsors, 21 were Republicans and 2 were Democrats [S4]; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would exempt them from strict liability for dangerous products they sell, cutting their litigation and insurance exposure [S3]. The gain comes directly out of injured customers' ability to recover from the seller [S2][S3].
Fewer claims against seller clients means fewer payouts and lower premiums for the insurance lines covering retail liability [S3].

Manufacturers' own liability rules are unchanged [S2], but with sellers exempt they would become the sole target in many suits — while an overall smaller litigation environment against the distribution chain works in their favor.
